---
title: "SentenceTransformers Embeddings"
guide-section: "Building a Store"
---

[sentence-transformers](https://www.sbert.net) is a popular Python library for computing text embeddings on your own machine. Instead of sending text to a web API, it downloads a model once and then runs it locally on your CPU or GPU. There's no API key to manage, no per-token cost, and your documents and queries never leave your environment. That makes it a natural choice for sensitive or proprietary content, for working offline, or simply for experimenting without worrying about a bill.

raghilda's `EmbeddingSentenceTransformers` provider can use any model on the [Hugging Face Hub](https://huggingface.co/models?library=sentence-transformers) that's compatible with sentence-transformers, and there are thousands of them. This guide covers installation, choosing a model, running on a GPU, and configuring the task prefixes that some models expect.

## Installation

sentence-transformers is an optional dependency, since it pulls in PyTorch and can be a fairly large install. Use the `sentence-transformers` extra to get it:

```bash
pip install "raghilda[sentence-transformers]"
```

## Basic usage

```{python}
#| echo: false
from huggingface_hub.utils import logging as hf_logging
hf_logging.set_verbosity_error()
```

Creating a provider loads the model, and then you can embed text right away:

```{python}
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingSentenceTransformers

provider = EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(model="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
embeddings = provider.embed(["hello world", "testing embeddings"])
print(f"Number of embeddings: {len(embeddings)}")
print(f"Embedding dimensions: {len(embeddings[0])}")
```

The first time you use a model, sentence-transformers downloads it from Hugging Face and saves it in the local Hugging Face cache (usually `~/.cache/huggingface`). Later runs load it from the cache, so only that first run needs a network connection. The default `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` model is under 100 MB, so the download is quick, but larger models can take a while.

Using the provider with a store works the same way as with any other provider. The example below builds a small in-memory store from three short documents and searches it:

```{python}
from raghilda.store import DuckDBStore
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingSentenceTransformers
from raghilda.document import MarkdownDocument
from raghilda.chunker import MarkdownChunker

store = DuckDBStore.create(
    location=":memory:",
    embed=EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(),
)

chunker = MarkdownChunker()
docs = [
    MarkdownDocument(content="DuckDB is an in-process analytical database.", origin="doc1"),
    MarkdownDocument(content="Embeddings are dense vector representations of text.", origin="doc2"),
    MarkdownDocument(content="Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds LLMs in source material.", origin="doc3"),
]
for doc in docs:
    store.upsert(chunker.chunk(doc))

store.build_index()

chunks = store.retrieve("How do vector databases work?", top_k=2)
for chunk in chunks:
    print(chunk.text)
```

Every step there ran locally: the documents were embedded on your machine when they were upserted, and the query was embedded the same way when `retrieve()` was called.

## Choosing a model

The right model depends on your trade-off between quality, speed, and memory use. Here are a few well-known options:

| Model | Dimensions | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` | 384 | The default. Small, fast, and good enough for many tasks |
| `all-mpnet-base-v2` | 768 | Noticeably better quality, but slower |
| `intfloat/e5-base-v2` | 768 | Strong retrieval model. Expects query and passage prefixes |
| `BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5` | 1024 | A high-quality English model |
| `intfloat/multilingual-e5-large` | 1024 | Multilingual. Expects query and passage prefixes |

`all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is a sensible default while you're getting a pipeline working, since it's small enough to run quickly on a laptop CPU. Once things are working, it's worth trying a larger model on your own data to see whether the improvement in results is worth the extra time. The [MTEB leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard) compares models on retrieval benchmarks and is a good way to find candidates.

::: {.callout-note}
Some models on the Hub, such as `nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5`, require `trust_remote_code=True` to load. `EmbeddingSentenceTransformers` doesn't pass that option through, so stick to models that load without it. If you'd like to use one of those models, [Ollama](embedding-ollama.qmd) packages several of them in a form that works out of the box.
:::

## Choosing a device

By default, sentence-transformers picks the fastest device it can find: a CUDA GPU if one is available, then Apple Silicon's GPU, and otherwise the CPU. You can override this with `device=`:

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Force CPU
provider = EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(model="all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device="cpu")

# Use Apple Silicon GPU
provider = EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(model="all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device="mps")

# Use CUDA
provider = EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(model="all-MiniLM-L6-v2", device="cuda")
```

Leaving `device` unset is usually the best choice. One reason to set it is portability: if you set `device=` explicitly, that setting is saved with the store. A store created with `device="cuda"` will then try to use CUDA when reconnected, which fails on a machine without an NVIDIA GPU. When in doubt, leave it as `None` so each machine can pick its own device.

The `batch_size=` parameter (64 by default) controls how many texts are encoded together. On a GPU with plenty of memory, a larger batch can speed up ingestion. If you run out of memory, lower it.

## Task-specific prompts

Some models were trained to expect a short prefix on each input that tells them whether the text is a search query or a document to be searched. The E5 family is a common example: queries should start with `"query: "` and documents with `"passage: "`. Without these prefixes the models still work, but their retrieval quality drops.

The `prompts=` parameter lets you set a prefix for each `EmbedInputType`:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.embedding import EmbeddingSentenceTransformers, EmbedInputType

provider = EmbeddingSentenceTransformers(
    model="intfloat/e5-base-v2",
    prompts={
        EmbedInputType.QUERY: "query: ",
        EmbedInputType.DOCUMENT: "passage: ",
    },
)
```

Once prompts are configured, the provider adds the matching prefix to each text before encoding it. The store chooses the input type for you: chunks written with `upsert()` or `ingest()` use the `DOCUMENT` prefix, and the text you pass to `retrieve()` uses the `QUERY` prefix. You can also set just one of the two. For example, some BGE models only want an instruction prefix on queries.

The correct prefixes differ from model to model, so check the model card on Hugging Face before setting them. Models that don't mention prefixes (like the default `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) don't need them.

## Reconnecting to a store

The store saves the model name, batch size, and any `device` or `prompts` settings, so reconnecting restores an identically configured provider:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from raghilda.store import DuckDBStore

store = DuckDBStore.connect("docs.db")
```

Keep in mind that restoring the provider means loading the model, so `connect()` takes about as long as creating the provider did. If the model isn't in the local cache (for example, on a fresh machine), it'll be downloaded at this point.

## Parameters

`EmbeddingSentenceTransformers` takes four parameters. All of them are optional, and with no arguments the provider runs `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` on whatever device sentence-transformers detects:

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `"all-MiniLM-L6-v2"` | Model name or Hugging Face repo ID |
| `device` | `None` | Device to run on, such as `"cpu"`, `"cuda"`, or `"mps"`. Auto-detected if `None` |
| `batch_size` | `64` | Texts encoded per batch |
| `prompts` | `None` | Optional prefix strings keyed by `EmbedInputType` |

You'll most often set `model`, plus `prompts` when the model's card asks for task prefixes. Since there's no API key involved, every parameter is saved with the store. That's convenient for `prompts`, but it's also why leaving `device` unset is the safer choice for stores that move between machines. For the full API details, see the [`EmbeddingSentenceTransformers` reference page](/reference/embedding.EmbeddingSentenceTransformers.qmd).
